utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the problem is the witness is waiting and that's -- it was perhaps premature to ask the witness to come in. I suggest that we give the witness an opportunity to have a cup of coffee and not to attend. Mr. Avramovic, there are still a few matters pending in relation to your written statement and to some other matters. I had hoped that we would resolve them in one or two minutes. I'm afraid it takes a bit more. I think it's better to allow you to leave the courtroom for a while and we'll call you back as soon as we are done with it. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Avramovic. And I apologise, Mr. Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, five minutes for you -- on the ballistic issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I may be able to do it in even less than five minutes. Your Honours will have seen the submissions of the Prosecution in this respect. We would respectfully submit that in order for any of this material to be fairly tested, and therefore to be capable of being fairly admitted at trial, it is necessary for the basis for an opinion to be explored, that is, we would respectfully submit, is a fundamental prerequisite for the admission fairly of evidence of opinion. Now, in this instance what the Prosecution propose to adduce through this particular witness is the contents of annex 66 to his witness statement, which really represents nothing more than a further statement from the witness about reports he claims to have read. Of those reports, the only one which is available to the Defence is the report which is annexed to the motion, dated the 2nd of December, 1998, from Captain Milutin Visnjic. That report, as Your Honours are aware, refers to a comparison between 14 cartridges found on the -- during the course of the September 1998 investigation in the canal area with ultimately 24 cartridges which are recorded as having been found in the village of Gramaqel on the 24th of March. This witness, in effect, seeks to suggest that he knows that the author of that report didn't mean Gramaqel, he meant Gllogjan, notwithstanding that there was a police operation in the entirety of that area on the 24th of March and that Gllogjan is separated from Gramaqel by Shaptej and Dubrave. He's not in a position to give that evidence; only the author of the report could give that evidence. And only the author of the report could give that evidence by reference to the material that was submitted to him and upon which he expressed that conclusion. None of that material is available or has been exhibited nor is it explained by the author of the reported. Now, the first objection here is what this witness is doing in annex 66 and what the Prosecution seek to elicit from him is a glosso-interpretation on a report written by someone else which says something different than that which he says it says and which is unsupported by any material which is capable of building the bridge by reference to contemporaneous records. So that is point one in terms of fair admission. Point two is that none of the working materials from which this Trial Chamber could make any evaluation of the reliability of the opinion expressed by Captain Visnjic even were his report to say what Mr. Avramovic wrongly says it says. None of the contemporary material or the workings is available for inspection nor can it be fairly tested by the Defence nor evaluated by the Trial Chamber. There is no expression of analysis as to the basis directly for the comparisons, as to whether they are individual or collective comparisons or as to whether or not the -- what the likelihood of coincidence is or the recurrence of those types of markings. But more fundamentally, none of this can be evaluated. It can't be evaluated because there is nothing more than a conclusion in Captain Visnjic's report with no workings or base material to explore. None of the notes are available, there is no second-opinion report and none of the casings can be compared. The net result is leaving -- there are essentially two groups of objections, either of which in our submission should result in the exclusion of this material. The first is there is no basis for building the bridge which Mr. Avramovic wishes to build in order to contradict the report upon which he relies as to where the casings from which the comparison is drawn were found. But more fundamentally even if that bridge could be built, the net result is the material can't be tested and therefore the validity of the conclusion can't be evaluated. Now, the Prosecution recognise in their motion in response the weaknesses of this material, but seek to suggest that the admissibility threshold set by the Tribunal's jurisprudence establishes a bar so low that they are able to get over it by merely asserting that a conclusion exists, because that's what this evidence amounts to. We respectfully submit that any reasonable Trial Chamber viewing this material as it stands would inevitably come to the conclusion that nil probative weight could be attached to it, if the conclusions cannot be fairly evaluated. And if that is the position, it ought not, in our submission, to be admitted because material which is of nil probative value is not material which in our submission satisfies the threshold of relevance. But more fundamentally there is an 89(C) objection as to the fairness of admitting material that cannot be properly tested or evaluated. So it's not simply sufficient for the Prosecution to fall behind the mantra that this is a matter of weight. In order for fair evaluation to take place, as a matter of fair trial requirements, in our submission, the foundation material must be available so that a conclusion can be assessed and the Trial Chamber can determine what weight appropriately to attach to it. And if the appropriate weight can't be fairly evaluated, then the evidence can't in our submission be fairly admitted. So we respectfully submit that the Prosecution's response misses the point and it is, and never can be, an answer in a situation such as this to say the Defence can cross-examine upon it, which is really the last refuge of the desperate advocate in the context of an argument like this, because how can the Defence cross-examine upon it, one asks rhetorically. The Defence can't possibly cross-examine upon it because the material upon which such cross-examination would be based has not been served and is not available. So anything which would go to an evaluation of the weight to be attached to it is simply unavailable to the Defence and unavailable to the Trial Chamber. And shorn of that material, this is evidence with no probative weight whatsoever but very considerable potential for unfairness. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I take it when you referred to the fairness requirement under Rule 89(C) that you were referring to 89(D)?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because 89(C) deals with the probative value. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have joined in the submissions made by Mr. Emmerson, and in addition wish to remind the Chamber that we also have filed an objection to the report itself. So we are in a position where not only do we adopt those arguments made, but also procedurally we are in a position where it would be inappropriate for the Chamber to consider that report given the nature in which it was recently forwarded to the court on June 28th as an expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we support the arguments advanced by Mr. Emmerson. We discussed these matters in detail outside the court, and we join, in its entirety, with his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, any additional submissions to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have listened with great care to the comments made by the Defence, and indeed they came back to the arguments that were presented in the motion that they submitted to exclude ballistic evidence. The information provided by Mr. Avramovic in annex 66 and that apparently we would not be able to evaluate such conclusions. As regards the argument relating to the bridge, indeed, there's nothing artificial in Mr. Avramovic's note, which was drafted several years ago. It's not a recent document and it's fairly commonplace for the police to draft such summary records, including the various evidence, the various elements of evidence, that they have collected in such an inquiry. This is normal procedure and this was explained in the second addendum which was presented last Thursday where it is stated how and why he went from the name Gramocelj to Glodjane and why Gramocelj was mentioned in one report and Glodjane in the other. I'm not going to go back to the substance because you're informed of these matters. They were -- information was given to both parties. As regards the second argument relating to the ballistic evidence that it's a mere conclusion, this is the best evidence possible which is available to the Prosecution; and therefore, we presented this under Rule 94 bis in Milutinovic and decided that we would be able to ask any questions that were related, questions that the Defence has just mentioned. So we believe that at this point, from the point of view of admissibility, of course it's up to the Chamber to decide after cross-examination, to determine the relative importance of this report and the explanations that are to be given by Mr. Visnjic, and therefore I do not agree with the points made by the Defence regarding the ballistic evidence. As regards the other issues, Mr. President, sir, I have developed the arguments in my response and I do not intend to repeat those here this morning because everyone has knowledge of those arguments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think there may be an error on the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Dutertre, isn't it true that the Visnjic report is an attachment to the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report is annexed to the 92 ter statement made by Mr. Avramovic, today's witness, but it's also annexed to the hearing -- the Visnjic hearing. So it's both in the 92 ter statement and the ballistics report as well. It's annex 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From a procedural point of view, if we would admit the 92 ter statement you could just withdraw the application for the report to be admitted under 94 bis, isn't it, because it's in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be a possibility. I shall leave it up to the Chamber to decide, given the fact that the Defence did express the desire to perhaps cross-examine Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered all arguments. The Chamber will now give its rulings, but not the full reasons. We would like to formulate them in detail. The Chamber - and I'm exclusively now talking about the ballistics, nothing else - the Chamber does not exclude the evidence of Mr. Avramovic in relation to the ballistics as we find it in the paragraphs mentioned by you, Mr. Emmerson, but the Chamber does not admit the Visnjic report as an attachment to that. There is an application for the admission of the Visnjic report under Rule 94 bis. Objections have been made in that respect, among them that Mr. Visnjic does not qualify as an expert. The Chamber will consider those objections, but the Chamber has already made up its mind that if it will admit the report, it will certainly grant the Defence the right to cross-examine Mr. Visnjic. So therefore, any suggestion that this report could be -- could be admitted without Mr. Visnjic appearing as a witness is rejected. It may be that before finally deciding on the admission of the Visnjic report the Chamber will invite the parties to make further submissions; that is a possibility. The parties will hear from us. We'll give our reasons in more detail. Just in order to avoid any misunderstanding, the mere fact that a witness writes down in a report that he tells us that in report so-and-so an expert -- or I don't know whether it's an expert, in a certain report some conclusions are drawn, does not mean that the Chamber, on the basis of that, would just accept that as being the full truth. At the same time, the Chamber is aware that it -- excluding the evidence now might cause us problems to overlook the whole of the evidence presented at the end of the case and we are usually evaluating the evidence in the context of the totality of the evidence presented. I do not further expand on the reasons. You'll hear about them in more detail. That is as far as the ballistics are concerned. Now, what remains are the relevant portions, and let's go through them one by one; I'm afraid that's the only possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Chamber please advise me as to what has to be drafted for the main hearing and the addendum. I see that under paragraph 197, I understood that we were to delete the last sentence, but for the rest it was a bit more complicated for the other addendum. Could I have the Chamber's instructions as to how we could redraft this appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unclear what you mean by that we have to delete the last sentence. Is that what the Chamber ruled?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In annex 63 of paragraph 197 there's a reference to the ballistics report. I am not absolutely certain what you want the Prosecution to redact, given the decision that you have just made. The draft -- what you want us to draft regarding the decision you've made, that is, for the main hearing as for the second addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find my way in this rather chaotic situation. The second addendum is about the Gramocelj-Glodjane issue. Is that -- I'll just get it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't got a hard copy with me, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, it's not quite clear to me, as a matter of fact. I've -- you made reference to annex 63 of paragraph 197. Let's just have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This annex is, indeed, the ballistics report of Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I've got an incomplete version of -- 197, where do I find that exactly in the 92 ter statement? It goes to 193 for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's paragraph 187, 187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That already resolves one matter. In 187, reference is made to the Visnjic report. As we said, the annex is not admitted. That means what the witness says here is at this moment -- well, to say in the air. It's just something which is not supported by that material. At least if we would make a redaction here, we would not even know that - and I don't think that that's the problem, that there exists a report - but at least what it now says, last line is that it did not specify the casings, which might be good reason not to accept findings, we don't know yet. So the Chamber did not give you any instruction at this moment. The Chamber, as a matter of fact, wants further to consider whether or not to admit the report not as an annex to this statement, but as a 94 bis statement. The Chamber has not made up its mind yet, may ask for further submissions. And again, one thing is clear, that that report where the author is known should not play a role without Mr. Visnjic being present to be cross-examined. And I am aware, Mr. Emmerson, that you consider cross-examination could not be effective under the present circumstances. So therefore no further instructions as far as that is concerned at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might I, just picking that point up and Mr. Dutertre's issue, might I just invite Your Honours' attention to paragraph 189, which is essentially the paragraph to be read with addendum number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- in which this witness purports to re-read annex 6 -- the -- the original crime scene report, and there was the Visnjic report, as referring not to Gramaqel but to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In other words, paragraph 189 is him interpreting a document which Your Honours currently do not admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it goes without saying. If we would have to go through it line by line and say here a reference is made, there a reference is made, I think the line of the Chamber may be clear, that we are not taking out a semicolon here, an "A" there, a letter "3" there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that if we would consider that the Visnjic report assists in a way as to be admitted, the Chamber then -- of course these references may play a role there; if not, then of course they are just without -- I mean, giving comment on something we have not -- explicitly not admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course then that comment will be ignored by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. So admitted, so to speak, pro tem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be at a later stage if we would decide that Mr. Visnjic is not an expert or if we would decide the report is non-admissible because for whatever reason it's late, then of course all parties could apply and say would you please take out this or would you please take out that as well. Whether there's any need to do so, of course I understand that if you want to perform your duties that you might insist on that. At the same time, the Chamber is -- as you may have noticed before, the Chamber is looking at substance rather than at form, although lawyers never should ignore the form. Is that clear by now? Then let's go through the -- let's try to resolve that as quickly as possible. I do understand that paragraph 11 has not been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see that the essential nature of the objection follows the objections as taken with prior witnesses in a similar category, that where generalisations and conclusions are drawn and if they're tendered to show the basis for an investigation or the witness's area of responsibility, then it is our submission that they are not admissible as evidence of the truth of their contents. And paragraph 11 is essentially unsourced generalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do it one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, could you tell us under what 65 ter number the consolidated witness statement is introduced in the report so that the other Judges are, to the extent that they have no hard copy with them, able to follow it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's number 65 ter 1401, 1401. The two addendums, if I may, are 1496 and 1497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- as far as paragraph 11 is concerned, the Chamber denies the objection. At the same time, Mr. Dutertre, if you would not give more detailed factual foundation for it, the evidence might not be of much support for the Prosecution's case. Next paragraph is 13. I gave a suggestion yesterday, Mr. Dutertre, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, the Prosecution is not opposed to that suggestion, that is, that there be a constructive debate; and therefore, we accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you changed your mind since yesterday? Is that -- but, Mr. Emmerson, you had more I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours will see my concern --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and it may be that it falls within the rubric of the observation that Your Honours have just made in relation to the paragraph 11, but my concern in addition is the sentence reading -- or that passage of the sentence which reads: "When the last remaining Serbs were expelled or kidnapped from Decan and the area on both sides of the Gjakove-Decan-Peje road," and then certain villages are given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That again, in our submission, in the absence of specific material when the Trial Chamber has heard specific evidence is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, then it will not surprise you that the Chamber will say -- take the same position there that further factual foundation has to be laid. Or at least that, Mr. Dutertre, that is what would -- would improve the support this evidence could give to the Prosecution's case. Then we take out: "The armed conflict started around 21st/22nd of April ..." And you redact it in such a way, Mr. Dutertre, that the date is kept: "... is the date on which the last remaining Serbs or kidnapped or expelled from Decan," and we will hear from the witness how he knows that this happened at those days. But "the armed conflict" and "the start of the armed conflict" is taken out. I take it you find the appropriate redaction for that. Then we move on to paragraph 32. The issue on 32 was last two sentences: "From the description of the victim given by Kalamashi crime inspectors who were interviewing him made conclusions about the identity of this person. I'm not sure if their conclusions were that the victim was Milovan Vlahovic or Milos Radunovic." This actually says: Conclusions were drawn, what the conclusions were, I do not know. That's -- I don't know, Mr. Dutertre, to what extent you think that unknown conclusions could support your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards this passage, the witness remembers that conclusions were drawn by others and everyone, therefore, recognises the speculative nature of such comments and it's up to the Chamber to evaluate the sentence as such. And the last sentence that's correlated with it indicates that it could have been one or the other victims. It does indeed show that the testimony is somewhat fuzzy, but I don't think it's inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the probative value? What could we conclude from this? Because you are saying that it's evaluation rather than -- now, what does this prove, that it could be these two persons, just as it could be everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, according to what the witness stated and the way I understood it, this means that according to the crime inspector's conclusions, it was one or the other of these two individuals that was the victim. The Prosecution, however, is not going to make a major point out of these two sentences, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last two lines have to be redacted, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I be permitted one tangential observation at this point. I haven't raised it as a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have dealt now with the last two sentences. They are out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They are out. Thank you very much. And the first nine sentences of the next paragraph cover the same territory. But may I mention one matter at this stage which relates to both of these objections. I have not sought to object, and neither have those representing either of the co-accused, to the admission through this witness, of the witness statements allegedly recorded as having been made by Bekim Kalamashi during this course of his detention. And plainly, rather like the passages of the witness statement that was sought to be tendered by the investigator, Mr. Haverinen, those passages have been understood by the Defence as being tendered not to show the truth of their contents but to show the purpose and the progress of the investigation; in other words, to justify the decision to go to the canal. And it is on that basis that no application has been made to exclude those statements themselves, a proper examination of them is a matter which may assist the Trial Chamber, but not, as we submit, as being potentially evidence of the truth of their contents, not least because the maker of the statement has disavowed the truth of the contents, but leaving that aside, it would not, in our submission, be appropriate for those statements to be admitted on that basis. So the passages that we are now dealing with, and Your Honours have just excluded the last two sentences of paragraph 32, are expressions of opinion by somebody other than the witness, reported by the witness as to what statements are being admitted not as to the truth of their contents properly meant at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me. Let me re-read the ... With the same caveat as given before, the first nine lines of paragraph 33 are not excluded. We move on to paragraph 96. Last sentence: "It seemed to be used as some kind of prison and also used as training area." That clearly is opinion, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would say that perhaps it's at the boundary between opinion and observation. It results from the various objects that the witness saw on the site. In addition, he is a police officer, a crime investigator, and he makes a comment on the basis of things that he saw and took note of. So I don't think it's inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about the last line of 96. We find in 97 what seems to be a more factual description. Could we not leave the opinion out and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last line of 96 is excluded. At the same time, may I add to that to the Defence that, of course, if a witness comes to the conclusion that in Europe it's light at night and dark during the day, then of course if you would leave it in, that would not necessarily mean that the Chamber would follow such opinions and conclusions. And this is obviously not a conclusion the Chamber would accept until and unless it would reach on the basis of the facts presented to it the same conclusion. Then we are at 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honours passed over the second sentence of 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm -- that's the -- if I may say the Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As regards the sentence in paragraph 97, I suggest that I will ask additional questions to the witness, as I stated in the response I sent yesterday to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We excluded, and of course you are entirely free to ask any questions about the witness which would give support to what is here presented as a conclusion. So that's excluded. Then we have paragraph 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution also believes that paragraph 98 is based on elements that were observed by the witness from the point where he was situated, in particular in paragraph 99 the witness observed targets, when he comments the video that he was shown he could see the targets. So this insertion in paragraph 98 is based on objective elements, based on things that the witness saw on site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether the Chamber would reach the same conclusions. Mr. Dutertre, paragraph 98 should be redacted in such a way that the facts remain, that is, that behind the farm that the witness located an area where there was several obstacles erected; and further, that there was an area with barbed wire. If you would like to ask the witness whether looking at this it brought something in his mind and what it brought into his mind and why it brought it in his mind, then you are free to do so. It could be that a comparison of the facts he observed here with, for example, facts he observed earlier in his life when he saw military educational training compounds, that's fair, but not to be presented in this way as a -- as an opinion which you, as a matter of fact, invited the Chamber to put everything together and to see whether all the factual elements -- and I do understand that we have to first look at 99 and only then at 98 in order to understand that where there is an area where obstacles are erected that gives the impression of a training ground. I can tell you that I know of a lot of areas where obstacles are erected which do not remind me of a military training ground. So there best be more and you can explore that matter when examining the witness. Then we have paragraph 170, I think, but there was -- it was not entirely clear to me what the remaining issue there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. If I can assist with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution have agreed to confine -- sorry, let me make it absolutely clear. The objection begins at the end of the first sentence after the bracketed reference to annex 68. The Prosecution have agreed to remove the remainder of that paragraph, except for the following sentence: "Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes ..." And the next-but-one sentence: "Isuf Hoxaj went missing in the Dulje pass between Prizren and Stimlje." Now, first of all, as far as the first of those two sentences are concerned, the Defence would accept that if the witness is in a position to lay a proper evidential foundation for that, then the information in itself is capable of being admitted. But in order to know whether that is the case, it's a matter which, in our submission, should properly be explored orally rather than through a 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we're talking about the first sentence which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crime ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as the second sentence is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That he went missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In a particular location. In our submission that ought not to be admitted. It ought not to be admitted because on any view it cannot be information that is capable of being reliable. Apart from anything else, the words that follow make it clear that the witness has no real information to give. He doesn't know when it happened, he thinks it was the beginning of 1998, he doesn't remember the circumstances, he doesn't know whether he went missing with Hajrulah Gashi or not. In itself, that information, which in any event, is inconsistent with the testimony of Witness 8, in our submission, ought not to be admitted on any basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if everything that is inconsistent with Witness 8, would that have to be excluded? There you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Emmerson, I don't know whether that's really what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Parenthetically, at the end of the submission I was making, I was drawing your attention to the place described is not the place that Your Honours have heard evidence about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Be that as it may, what is clear from what is set out in this witness statement is that there is nothing that the witness is able to give which is capable of materially assisting the Trial Chamber to understand the evidence surrounding the disappearance of those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I do intend to ask supplementary questions to the witness as regards to the origin of the information mentioned in the first sentence, that is, that Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes. I don't really see that there's any major difference in nature between that and the second sentence, and of course I can put questions to the witness to ask him how he learned that Isuf Hoxaj disappeared. I can ask him such questions and I don't see what makes this information inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, to be -- to be quite clear, so the Defence proposes to take out: "He was a sort of a con man and was often seen in the company of policemen. He was probably killed because of being a police informant." That to be taken out, to be excluded. And then the next line: "In," but then to exclude all the remainder or at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you said: "Isuf Hoxaj went missing," that should be excluded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I can take it from the beginning: "Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes," we would respectfully submit that is most appropriately dealt with once it is clear whether the witness has an evidential foundation from which to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The next two sentences: "He was a sort of a con man and he was probably killed ..." It is agreed that that should be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The following sentence, given what follows, is of no evidential value to the Trial Chamber and the information that follows on from that: "I don't know when he went missing ... " is -- and to the end of the paragraph is agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not quite sure what the Defence is suggesting to keep or to remove. I thought that the Defence accepted that we keep the first sentence: "Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes," the rest would be deleted, and that there was still disagreement as regards the sentence: "Isuf Hoxaj went missing in the Dulje pass between Prizren and Stimlje," and now I must say I'm a bit confused as to what has been decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not confused. The Chamber has not decided anything yet but will now do so. Paragraph 170, excluded are the two sentences: "He was a sort of a con man and was often seen in the company of policemen. He was probably killed because of being a police informant." The remainder including the sentence: "Isuf Hoxaj went missing in the Dulje pass between Prizren and Stimlje," is not excluded. At the same time, Mr. Dutertre, where the witness explains in rather -- in some detail at what he does not know, the Chamber, of course, in order to accept the place where Isuf Hoxaj was missing on the basis of this evidence would certainly need to know on what basis the witness states that Isuf Hoxaj went missing in that specific place. Then I think we dealt with all the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I take this just very brief moment to make one observation. I think none of us wishes to use the Trial Chamber's valuable time in editing witness statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact what I suggest for the next time is I call you at 10.00 at night, hear from you whether you have reached any conclusion, have someone available who will put everything on the record and we'll do it between 10.00 and 12.00 at night and not between quarter past 9.00 until a quarter past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I make perhaps an additional and alternative suggestion, which is that given that these are 92 ter statements and that they, therefore, represent material which can perfectly properly be admitted orally, if there is to be any doubt -- and it must be clear now to the parties and certainly to the Prosecution what the natures of the objections and the likely rulings will be, if there is any doubt about a passage in the witness statement there is nothing to stop the Prosecution excluding it from the 92 ter statement and eliciting it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: None of us wishes to be in the position, as I say, of using the Trial Chamber's time to conduct an exercise which is essentially arid because the material can be dealt with just as well orally as it can in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I fully do agree that we would have needed less than an hour to elicit the evidence as you would have sought to have it admitted, Mr. Dutertre, on paper, to elicit it orally from the witness. May the witness be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, I hope that you had some coffee. Mr. Avramovic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration which you gave at the beginning of your testimony, which until now was not on matters of substance for the case. You'll now be examined by Mr. Dutertre, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Would you like me to present the witness statement, although they have not been redacted as of yet under 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... portions not admitted, that does not mean that the attestation, that is, whatever he said -- well, I'm not going to anticipate on what the attestation will be, but that could be made for the statement in its entirety and then admission would be limited to the parts we discussed before. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One other question, or rather, a comment. You have a consolidated version in Serb language, you have the English translation, and there are two addendums. In addition to that, and all of these documents have been sent to the Chamber, there's also an index which enables you to find your way through the various annexes and the pages and paragraphs under the 65 ter statement. Now, as regards these annexes, from a technical point of view, you recall that for Mr. Sefa [sic], a previous witness, these annexes were physically annexed to the consolidated statement and that they all received an exhibit number, which was not a problem because this was the only witness making statements regarding those annexes. In this case, however, several witnesses have been questioned on these annexes and others will in the future also do so, which is why I suggest that each of the annexes be given a separate exhibit number; and in order for us to keep things straight, that there be a clear numbering so that the Prosecution and the Defence not have to go wading through the document system in order to find the appropriate documents that have been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I take it that that causes no specific difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar would like to have the list. She'll check whether she received it already or otherwise -- Madam Registrar has not received the list. The staff of the Chamber has received it, so if you would please provide Madam Registrar with the list and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Indeed, we're removing annex 63 from the list. I believe I asked -- I gave the usher two binders with the main statement, the annexes, and the addendums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please now proceed, because we would like to hear the testimony of the witness, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Avramovic, in May/June 2007 you gave a consolidated statement, where you referred to certain annexes, and a supplementary statement. These documents are to be found in the binders that are being placed in front of you. Do you recognise these statements, the annexes, as being the statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The questions that were put to you during the session, if you were to be asked the same questions today, would you respond in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Does this represent a true and faithful version of your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm now going to ask you various questions. When you respond, you are, in fact, responding to the Chamber, so please do look at the Judges. Mr. Avramovic, my first question relates to paragraph 170 of your consolidated statement, the main statement in which, and I quote the statement: "Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes." I would like to ask you, please refer to the written copy of your statement, I'd like to ask you how you know that Isuf Hoxaj was a police informant for petty crimes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this from conversations with my colleagues who worked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of the colleagues with whom you had those conversations?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall their names, but these are colleagues from the crime police. They are crime inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where were these colleagues based?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And where did you have these conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my work-place in the Djakovica police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Before you left Kosovo in 1999. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Dutertre repeat the question, please. There was an overlap with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Avramovic, what exactly were the words that your colleagues used as regards Mr. Isuf Hoxaj?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an informant of the service in relation to some petty crimes, burglaries, forced entries into shops, and so on and so forth, and he would inform the police about the identities of the perpetrators of these crimes. And he would often socialise with them, he would be in their company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Well, when you said he spent time with them, you mean he spent time with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another sentence in paragraph 170 and I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "Mr. Isuf went missing in the Dulje pass between Prizren and Stimlje."

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was officially recorded in the report submitted by his family, which stated that he went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that it was his son who reported him missing, if I recall that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no interpretation of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... But I see that on page 32, line 5, the question was not interpreted but at the same time I see that the witness either continued his answer or answered the question. Could you please repeat that portion of the question and answers, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. The question on line 3, page 32 was whether or not the witness has access to the report himself. And the second question on line 5 was whether he remembers anything else about that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So apparently it has been translated into the language of the witness, but there appears no translation in English, and that already starts at page 31, line 25. Now, those who are listening to the English channel, have they received interpretation of these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the last question was the only one I did not receive interpretation of, but the answer made it clear what the question had been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not try to fully explore what is a transcription problem and what's an interpretation problem. Let's proceed. It seems that the witness has -- from the gist of his answers, I take it that he has understood the question. Perhaps you summarize it for him, Mr. Dutertre, and then we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Again, the last question was whether or not the witness remembers any other details regarding the report that he himself had access to. This was the question in line 5, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You stated that the son reported that he had gone missing. Do you remember anything else?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only thing I remember. I don't recall any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I'm looking at the clock. We'll have a break. Would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, no problems. This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Avramovic, we'll have a break for close to half an hour, and -- but I have one or two questions remaining for Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, since you suggested to tender all the annexes, annex 65, that is the case file and the report on the attack in Pljancor against Maslovare. The report says that it's with 16 photographs; I find only 12, not necessarily to be dealt with at this very moment, but perhaps you would check that in the break. Then may I draw your attention -- what you see at the same time in this -- in this report is that the sketch attached to it, the sketch of the crime scene, that the legenda are properly translated. However, if I look at annex 64, which is the report on -- well, let's say 24th of March events, there I find several sketches. But I found only in relation to one of them the key, and all the others are without. I wonder how you would imagine the Chamber to understand those sketches without having a translation. If you could please clarify this after the break. Then we'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, before we continue, two observations. First of all, the list of annexes to the 92 ter statement describes the -- the documents as attachment so-and-so without giving a proper description. It's very difficult to find your way through it. That's one. Then second, I see that you've old ERN numbers, new ERN numbers. It is very confusing that in the 92 ter statements you're referring to old ERN numbers that are not the ERN numbers that appear as the last ones accepted, but usually to the ones stricken out. I don't know what's the purpose of giving new ERN numbers and striking out the previous one and then striking out again the number before that. It confuses me. I don't know what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards the second comment, the reason is that during the witness statement we presented the documents with the old ERN number and they were then recompiled so that a new ERN was given to the annexes. That's why in the document -- in the index you find both the old ERN and the new ERN number, but in fact at the time when the statement was taken we only had the old ERN number. It was only thereafter that a new number was given to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, but when I'm reading a statement and when reference is made to the ERN numbers, then I first have to go to that list to find the new ERN numbers. And I always was under the impression that the ERN numbers were to identify -- to give a unique identification of a document. Now, what's the sense of adding new ERN numbers where the document is identified by the old one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's simply because the whole -- all of these various documents were put into a new package, and therefore -- in fact, some of the annexes had handwritten markings and represented new exhibits. And that is why a new ERN number was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still -- I see that, of course on the document you write "annex 59," which of course is -- I mean, if the document is identified with sufficient precision, I also see that then the -- the investigator again signs that document. What the use of all that is entirely unclear to me, but -- so to the extent it can be avoided, please do so. Then do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do so in the future, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have further information about the two issues I raised, that's the 16 and the 12 photographs and the translation of the sketches -- at least the keys to the sketches in the 24th of March, 1998, investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, as regards the photographs, a number of them are missing. Having checked the system, it seems that the original document does not include those photographs. We must, however, check in the evidence section whether or not the documents include those photographs or not or whether they're only accessible on a screen and whether that is the explanation for the reason why those photographs, those three or four photographs, are not included. We are continuing our research. When we tried to open the document with the present ERN number, the photographs do not appear. As regards your question regarding translation, we are checking. Apparently these translations are not available, but we are doing our best so that the translations will be provided to the Chamber and to the Defence as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. The Chamber would highly appreciate it. If by reading these documents we find the shortcomings on first reading, it surprises a bit that where you have thoroughly, I take it, investigated these documents that this did not come to your mind. Please proceed now. Mr. Avramovic, we'll continue to hear your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, I have a few questions for you regarding paragraph 11 of your statement. You stated that in January and February 1998, many civilian cars were attacked while travelling at night on the Djakovica-Pec road. Could you tell us how you know that bit of information.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I participated in many investigations into those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many investigations you participated in regarding attacks on civilian cars on that road?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually inspected several vehicles that had been attacked during that period. I performed on-site inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just to clarify your own -- that clarifies your role in these investigations, but how many investigations are we referring to? How many investigations did you participate in regarding these events?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in several, five or six maybe, but I know that my colleagues also participated in several investigations of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many events, to your knowledge, how many attacks occurred in the months of January and February on civilian cars on that road?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there must have been a dozen or so or even maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Avramovic, you have stated in paragraph 11 in your statement that the victims were Serbs and that after a while the police discovered that the Albanians who travelled at night, in order to be recognised as Albanians and not be attacked, left the inside light on in their cars. And therefore, those vehicles, when the light was on, were not attacked. Could you tell the Court how you found out about that information?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from my colleagues who had become privy to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of your colleagues who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At what point in time did you learn about this information from your colleagues? I understand you don't remember their names, but do you remember when they told you about this, what period of time it was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that somewhat later, maybe a month or two months after the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did your colleagues obtain this information, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this was in the interviews with the members, or rather, terrorists who had been captured, I suppose so. That's the most plausible explanation I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show a video sequence from the video V00-601, 20.24, 1 minute and 59 seconds. We're going to be showing this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... text being spoken?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you provided the booth with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. Have you oriented yourself to the procedure followed in this courtroom as far as sound or videos is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe the transcript has been given to the interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before playing it, would you please do so, because otherwise we can't proceed. The procedure here is, Mr. Dutertre, and you should be aware of that, it should have been discussed within your team, that in order to have a full transcript in the two languages of this Tribunal, that the one interpreter follows on paper whether the text of the transcript reflects the words spoken, whereas the other interpreter, who most likely is not able to follow the speed of speech, translates on the basis of the written transcript so that we have a full transcript in both languages. That's the procedure that has been explained again and again, and I'm surprised that you have not been -- you have not prepared for this procedure to be followed. Therefore, it's of no use at this moment to play the video. If you please would prepare the transcript to the interpreters' booth so that we can do that at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very sorry. We're going to be transcribing the transcript very rapidly. I shall then go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it there is a written transcript, it's just a matter of printing out, isn't it, because if you have to start transcribing now, then that would cause --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the transcript exists. It's just a question of copying it and sending it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please take care that it will be there soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has received the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, from March 1998 until the end of August 1998, what information did you have, if you did have information, regarding the disappearance of individuals in the zone that you have described and sketched in annex 2, that is, a zone that was not safe for reasons of security?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that all Serbs who had remained in the territory had been kidnapped, also that anybody who attempted to enter the territory was also kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did the police receive such information?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the relatives of those who had gone missing, from various sources working for the service, and also from the terrorists who had been captured and brought in for interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many individuals from -- in the period March to August 1998, how many disappearances did you hear about? How many individuals had been said to have disappeared?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that all the Serbs who remained living in the territory had been kidnapped. We heard of all those instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, could we just clarify that. Does that mean that in the area there was no Serb remaining who had not been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was this -- this exercise completed then? I mean, on from what moment all Serbs had been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The end of April/beginning of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Did you say the end of April/beginning of May or beginning of March? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beginning of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to describe a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I misspoke. It was May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, how did you yourself learn about this information? You -- did you hear it from your colleagues? Did you read reports? Were there police meetings? What is the source of your knowledge, your own knowledge, of these kidnappings and disappearances?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several ways. I saw documents, reports, on the missing persons, and also in talking to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After this period of March, April, and May, were there other persons of ethnic origin other than Serb, not Serb, were there other disappearances in the same zone?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Albanians who were loyal to the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, do you remember the names of both Serbs and Albanians who disappeared during that period and that you yourself have knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the names. As I've already told you, those who remained in the territory who didn't manage to flee were the Radosevic family, the Radunovic family, two members of the Ministry of the Interior, Zdravko Radunovic. I can't remember all the names at the moment, but there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you mention two members -- two individuals who worked for the Ministry of the Interior, do you remember their names or not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was Rade Popovic and Nikola Jovanovic, and also Nenad Remistar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you refer to Albanians loyal to the government, what do you mean by that? You used that expression a moment ago in a previous answer; what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those Albanians did not want to take up the arms and fight against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Mr. Avramovic, I'm going on to another topic. In paragraph 41 and 42 of your statement, you explain that an investigation team was set up to go to the lake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Dutertre continues, I haven't objected during the course of that last passage of examination-in-chief to the absence of specificity or means of knowledge in respect of individual cases, either in respect of the Serbs or in respect of Albanians described. I haven't done so on the assumption that this is information which is being elicited, as before, in order to show the basis for investigation rather than as being tendered to show the truth of its contents. But plainly, if Mr. Dutertre wishes to rely as evidence for the truth of its contents on assertions of kidnapping, something more detailed by way of foundation would need to be laid. I forebear from objecting and interjecting, but on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, is that clear and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to understand that that applies to the whole series of questions I've put to the witness or just the last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I think you referred to the series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Join.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, did you participate in investigations of cases of kidnapping of Serbs or Albanians that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't participate because it was impossible to carry out on-site inspections in that period -- territory during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you explain why it is that it was impossible to carry out investigations in that territory.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that territory was under the control of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The knowledge, your personal knowledge, of these cases of disappearances, therefore, comes from the families having lodged complaints and your discussions with colleagues; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you have any other precise information on one of -- one of the other cases of disappearances that you mentioned earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. I did not understand your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of names, in particular two police officers of Serb origin who disappeared. Could you give us more detail about the cases of these two police officers?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the reports that were submitted at the time, we did not make any inquiries. I know that they went in the direction of Rastavica, as they were supposed to be transporting food supplies; they were on duty. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And how did you learn that those two individuals had disappeared, that is, those two precise individuals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learnt this from their superior officers, who reported them missing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: Can the other microphone for the witness be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, you mentioned the name of Nenad Remistar. Do you have any additional details regarding what happened to that person?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he was kidnapped as he was going back from his home in Glina, or rather, he was going to work and he was travelling along the Djakovica-Pristina road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is the source of that information, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report filed by his relatives and by his superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you read that report yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned the names Radunovic and Radosevic. Could you give us more details about what happened to those persons, and then I'll ask you afterwards how you learned about that information.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't able to leave their houses in the villages where they resided. They were kidnapped and their relatives reported them missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you speak to the family members yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, because their sons were also members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like now to discuss paragraphs 41 and 42 of your statement. You have stated that an investigation team was set up in order to go to the lake, and once the SUP had questioned the individuals who had been arrested on September 3rd. My question is as follows: Did the entire investigation team arrive at the same time or did you arrive one after the other in time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire investigation team, I indicated in this document, arrived at that site at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you discovered the bodies at the concrete wall at the end of the canal, how did you report this information to your hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably over the radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now to call up the video V0061 [as interpreted] from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you ask Mr. Dutertre to repeat the reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's video V000-6011, minute 3, 11 seconds to 3.36 seconds, and there's no transcript for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We normally can put it on, turn it on from here, but it doesn't seem to be running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on my e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please start the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we stop the video just there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, the object that we can see in the left corner of the video, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should back-track just a tiny bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recognise this. It is most probably a piece of timber or a stump or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue playing the video. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. [Interpretation] Can we back-track just a tiny bit. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, can you tell us when, what day, this video was taken?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably on the 11th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Well, was it the same day that the bodies were removed or was it before or after?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which bodies are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the initial phase of the investigation by the forensic specialists that came from Belgrade to remove the bodies, to examine the bodies.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the exhumation only started at that site, so probably this footage was made before the start of the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Avramovic. On this video that seems to be taken from the wooden bridge that crosses the canal, we cannot see the bodies discovered that were close to the wall, the bodies that were at the surface of the water. Can you tell us approximately at what part of the wall these bodies that were removed were found near the wall, that is, the bodies that were removed by the forensic specialists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm -- first of all, I don't understand the premise for the question. There's no evidence at all so far that bodies that were close to the wall were removed by forensic specialists. So if that is something that Mr. Dutertre wishes to put to this witness, it would be helpful to know the basis for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, Mr. Dutertre, you guided the witness to paragraphs 41 of his statement, where he describes how they decided to form a crime scene investigation. And then he describes in paragraph 42, 43, and then 44, I took it that this is in chronological order. And then in paragraph 44 he arrives at the canal at the 9th of September. So if you take him to 41, I'm a bit surprised that we suddenly are at the 11th of September. Could you please clarify that and could you also keep in mind what Mr. Emmerson just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In fact, I had gone on to another topic after the arrival of the team, and this video was filmed on the 11th. And in the witness statement at paragraph 118, the witness states that bodies were exhumed close to the wall of the canal. So, in fact, it's on the basis of the consolidated witness statement, indeed, for reasons of clarity I probably should have referred to paragraph 118 before I showed this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that apart from whether it was the 11th of September, Mr. Dutertre, you know that there is a bit of confusion about the date. So I would very much like you to -- to further verify what makes the witness think that this video was on the 11th, but apart from that I think Mr. Emmerson also complained about the bodies near to the wall being exhumed by experts, I think that was part of his problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I just make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's page 48, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question asks: "On this video that seems to be taken from the wooden bridge that crosses the canal, we cannot see the bodies discovered that were close to the wall, the bodies that were at the surface of the water. Can you tell us approximately at what part of the wall these bodies that were removed were found near the wall, that is, the bodies that were removed by the forensic specialists?" Now, the natural reading of that question is asking about the removal of the bodies that were found at the surface of the water close to the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As to which there has been no evidence of their removal; on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's been a mistake. I was referring to the bodies that were on the earthen side. In fact, I wanted the witness to indicate approximately where the bodies were that were found at the surface close to the wall of the canal on the earthen side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, Mr. Dutertre, then to talk about the bodies that were at the surface of the water does not clearly guide the witness to the -- to bodies that were not in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe that I said "surface." I don't believe I said that in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- I don't remember, as a matter of fact, but then please formulate your question again so that there could be no -- no confusion whatsoever. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, it would seem that this video is taken from the bridge that crosses the canal. On this picture here, you cannot see the bodies that were discovered at the surface on the earth alongside of the canal wall. And I'm referring here to the bodies that were found on the earth and not in the water. Can you tell us where those bodies found on the earth, where they were found on this picture?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were on the right-hand side of the canal next to the concrete wall, and I'm saying on the right-hand side of the canal, toward the end, as we see it here on the still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dutertre, just for the basis of your question, what paragraph of the statement you are actually referring to? Because you're now talking about bodies not in the water, along the water but on the earth, where do we find that in the statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
